stories.headline: Apple cites 'shocking evidence' of data destruction in OpenAI suit
stories.hook: Ex-employee Chang Liu allegedly told an OpenAI colleague to destroy evidence after Apple's probe began.
stories.tldr: Apple has filed new documents in its lawsuit against OpenAI, citing "shocking evidence" from the MacBook of former employee Chang Liu. The company argues this proves the urgent need for expedited discovery, claiming defendants ignored available data. According to the filing, Liu sent instructions to destroy evidence to an OpenAI colleague who confirmed she would comply upon learning of Apple’s internal investigation. This alleged coordination raises the stakes significantly, moving the case beyond mere IP theft into potential obstruction. The court now faces a decision on whether to accelerate the process before further digital assets are potentially lost or altered by the parties involved.

transcript.text: I was paged at 3 a.m. because the filing dropped. It’s not just about the code anymore; it’s about the cleanup. When you see someone instruct a third party to delete data after an internal probe starts, you know the chain of custody is broken. I’ve seen this playbook before: panic, purge, pray. But here, the prayer was answered by a colleague who said yes.

Look at the speed of the confirmation. Liu didn’t just do it himself; he outsourced the destruction. That implies a level of coordination that suggests this wasn’t a momentary lapse in judgment. It was a strategy. And if OpenAI knew, or should have known, they are complicit. You don’t ignore a direct instruction to destroy evidence when you’re sitting across the table from Apple.

body.text:
It is not real until it has survived a Tuesday in production, and right now, the production environment of this lawsuit is catching fire. I got the alert while half-asleep, which is usually when the most damning details surface. Apple’s latest filing isn’t just complaining about slow discovery; it’s presenting what it calls "shocking evidence" that directly supports their demand for expedited measures. The core issue revolves around Chang Liu, one of the parties named in Apple’s lawsuit, whose actions have escalated from alleged IP theft to active obstruction.

The specific detail that keeps me up at night isn’t the theft itself, but the reaction to it. Upon learning of Apple’s internal investigation, Liu didn’t just stop working; he reached out. He sent instructions for destroying evidence to an OpenAI colleague. Crucially, that colleague confirmed she would comply. In my world, when someone confirms they are going to break things, you assume they will. We run these simulations constantly. The failure isn’t in the detection; it’s in the prevention. Once the deletion instruction is sent, the window for recovery shrinks exponentially.

You are going to see this shift in tone immediately. This is no longer a dispute over who wrote which line of code. This is a criminal procedure problem wrapped in a civil suit. Apple is arguing that the "shocking evidence"—which they claim defendants chose to ignore despite its availability—demonstrates why they urgently need expedited discovery. Watch what happens next. The ball is in the judge’s court, but the pressure is on. If the court believes that evidence is being destroyed in real-time, the standard clock stops ticking. You don’t wait for a routine schedule when the house is burning down. This changes the leverage entirely. OpenAI can no longer play the long game of procedural delay. They have to engage with the forensic reality of the MacBook now.

There is a workaround nobody documents, but it’s simple: trust no one’s word, only the hash. When Liu sent those instructions, he created a paper trail that is arguably more damaging than the original trade secrets. The fact that an OpenAI colleague confirmed compliance is the smoking gun. It moves the liability from one rogue actor to the organization. I have seen teams try to scrub logs after an incident response call, and it always looks worse. Here, the scrubbing was premeditated and delegated. For Apple, this is the win they needed to justify the aggressive posture. It turns a messy IP fight into a clear-cut case of bad faith. The desk splits on the outcome, but not on the severity. This is a major escalation.

satire.setup: The standard legal timeline assumes all parties act in good faith and preserve data intact.
satire.payoff: When one party actively coordinates the destruction of evidence, the 'standard' timeline becomes a tool for hiding crimes rather than uncovering truth.
